reference.source: Braunwald's Heart Disease / ESC guidelines on cardiac tumours
clinicalPearls: The most common primary tumour of the cardiac valves and a leading benign valvular tumour, typically small and arising on valve surfaces
It has a characteristic frond-like, sea-anemone appearance with multiple papillary arms attached by a short stalk
The aortic valve is the most frequent site, followed by the mitral valve, and lesions are usually single
Many are found incidentally on echocardiography performed for other reasons
The principal clinical hazard is embolism, which can cause stroke, transient ischaemic attack, coronary embolism with angina or myocardial infarction, or peripheral events
The mobile tumour or associated thrombus on its surface is the embolic source, so mobility on imaging is an important risk marker
Transoesophageal echocardiography best characterises the lesion, and it must be distinguished from vegetation and thrombus
Surgical excision, usually with valve preservation, is considered for symptomatic, left-sided, or highly mobile tumours because of embolic risk
reference.pathophysiology: Papillary fibroelastoma is a benign avascular tumour of the endocardial surface, most often on the valves. It consists of a branching core of dense connective tissue rich in elastic fibres, covered by a layer of endothelium, giving the multiple frond-like papillary projections that resemble a sea anemone when immersed in fluid. The clefts between the fronds promote stasis and deposition of platelet-fibrin thrombus. Because the tumour and any adherent thrombus are mobile and exposed to flow, fragments can detach and embolise; left-sided lesions on the aortic or mitral valve threaten the cerebral, coronary, and systemic circulations.
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic and transoesophageal echocardiography to define the frond-like mobile valvular mass
Cardiac MRI in selected cases to further characterise the lesion
Blood cultures and inflammatory markers to help exclude infective endocarditis
Neuroimaging when cerebral embolism is suspected
Coronary assessment if there are features of coronary embolism
Histological confirmation of the excised specimen
redFlags: Stroke or transient ischaemic attack attributable to the lesion
Coronary embolism causing angina or myocardial infarction
Highly mobile left-sided tumour with high embolic potential
reference.prognosis: The tumour itself is benign and surgical excision is generally curative with a good outlook and low recurrence; the main determinant of prognosis is the embolic complications that occur before treatment.
pitfalls: Mistaking the lesion for an infective vegetation and initiating unnecessary prolonged antibiotics
Underestimating embolic risk in mobile left-sided lesions
Confusing it with benign Lambl's excrescences or valvular thrombus
Assuming an incidental finding is harmless without weighing embolic potential
references: Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
ESC guidance on the management of cardiac tumours
management: Surgical excision, valve-sparing where possible, as definitive treatment, particularly for left-sided, large or highly mobile lesions given the embolic risk
Prioritise excision in symptomatic patients and those who have already had an embolic event such as stroke, transient ischaemic attack, or coronary or peripheral embolism
Surveillance echocardiography for small, incidentally found, asymptomatic lesions when surgery is deferred
Antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy to reduce embolic risk in patients not undergoing immediate surgery
Exclude infective endocarditis with blood cultures before attributing a valvular mass to fibroelastoma
Histological confirmation of the excised specimen
